item.title: People urged to be vigilant after maggots found in BBQ bought from Valelevu roadside stall
item.description: People are being urged to be vigilant when buying food from roadside stalls after a couple found maggots in BBQ purchased from a stall in Valelevu, Nasinu, at around 1am today. The man has told fijivillage News he had already taken a few bites before discovering the maggots.
item.content:encoded:
People are being urged to be vigilant when buying food from roadside stalls after a couple found maggots in BBQ purchased from a stall in Valelevu, Nasinu, at around 1am today.

The man has told fijivillage News he had already taken a few bites before discovering the maggots.

Consumer Council of Fiji CEO Seema Shandil says finding maggots in food is a serious breach of food safety standards and indicates a possible breakdown in hygiene, storage or quality control.

Shandil says maggots in food are never normal and their presence may indicate that food has been contaminated or has been stale for several days.

She says roadside stalls and all food establishments have a responsibility to ensure the food they sell is safe, fit for purpose and fit for human consumption.

Shandil is advising consumers who find maggots in food to stop eating immediately and consider the entire product contaminated.

She says people should preserve the evidence by keeping the food in its original packaging where possible, taking clear photographs of the food, maggots and packaging, and keeping their receipt or proof of purchase.

She says people should also note the date, time and location of purchase and return to the retailer with the food, receipt and photographs to request a full refund or replacement.

Shandil says people should also report food safety concerns to the Consumer Council while concerns can also be reported to the Ministry of Health or the relevant Municipal Council.

Shandil says the food stalls in question operate after business hours and such matters are escalated to the Nasinu Town Council for inspection and any necessary enforcement action.

She says the Council is currently conducting surveillance of bakeries and restaurants and will soon extend this to roadside stalls.

However, Shandil says monitoring vendors who operate through the night and into the early morning hours presents significant challenges.

She is urging roadside food vendors to check their food, store it properly, protect it from flies and contamination, and throw away food that is not safe.

Questions have also been sent to the Nasinu Town Council.

item.title: Fiji records highest-ever World Press Freedom Index ranking, placed 24th globally
item.description: Fiji has achieved its highest-ever position in the World Press Freedom Index, ranking 24th out of 180 countries, with Reporters Without Borders (RSF) saying pressure on the media has eased since Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka took office. Fiji has risen from 102nd in 2022 to 24th in the latest World Press Freedom Index, improving from 40th in 2025 with its score increasing from 71.20 to 76.76.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji has achieved its highest-ever position in the World Press Freedom Index, ranking 24th out of 180 countries, with Reporters Without Borders (RSF) saying pressure on the media has eased since Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka took office.

Fiji has risen from 102nd in 2022 to 24th in the latest World Press Freedom Index, improving from 40th in 2025 with its score increasing from 71.20 to 76.76.

Fiji has also recorded strong results across the individual measures used by RSF, including ranking 10th in the world for the safety of journalists.

RSF says after 16 years of recurring attacks on press freedom by former Prime Minister Voreqe Bainimarama, pressure exerted on the media by civil and military authorities has eased since the election of Sitiveni Rabuka as head of the Republic of Fiji in 2022.

They say the repeal of the draconian and unpopular Media Industry Development Act (MIDA) in April 2023 is an important step forward.

RSF further says until recently, authorities used discriminatory advertising practices to blackmail the media, withholding ads and legal notices from those regarded as critical of the government.

They say for example, at the height of the pandemic, under the former FijiFirst government, the then pro-government Fiji Sun benefited from a preferential advertising allocation at the expense of its rival, the Fiji Times.

RFS says the latter was also banned from distribution in several parts of the country in 2020 on the grounds that “the press is a non-essential service”.

They also say journalists’ interests are represented by the Fijian Media Association, which was often critical of the harassment of the media by the previous FijiFirst government.

RFS says since the repeal of the Media Act in 2023, the FMA has worked hard to restore independent journalism and public trust in the media.

They say in March 2024, research published in Journalism Practice found that sexual harassment of women journalists was widespread and needed to be addressed to protect media freedom and quality journalism.

Meanwhile, the Government says they remain committed to protecting media freedom and freedom of expression and ensuring that a free and independent media continues to play its important role in Fiji’s democracy.
